stem: A platform team shares coding conventions through project CLAUDE.md and uses auto memory for developer preferences. A repository maintenance command may delete generated assets, but corporate policy permits it only when a local approval record matches the requested target. The same command text can be permitted or forbidden as that record changes. Which control should the architect add to evaluate the record before Claude Code executes the command, while retaining approved maintenance?

options.text: Use a PostToolUse command hook to compare the deletion target with the approval record and report a policy failure before Claude continues its next turn.
Add a permissions.deny pattern for the maintenance command so unapproved deletions are blocked, leaving the approval record to document permitted exceptions.
Put the approval-check procedure in a project skill and instruct Claude to invoke it before maintenance, retaining CLAUDE.md for conventions and auto memory for preferences.
Use a PreToolUse command hook to inspect the proposed target and approval record, denying the tool call when they do not match and otherwise leaving normal permissions in effect.

explanation: PreToolUse runs before tool execution and can return a deny decision. A command handler can inspect the proposed input and check the scenario's approval record before deciding, rather than relying on Claude to follow an instruction. A successful check can leave the ordinary permission flow unchanged. This is an execution-time check on the matched tool call, not a claim that hooks automatically recognize every destructive command. CLAUDE.md and auto memory remain useful context, not enforcement mechanisms.

distractorNotes.a: PostToolUse is suitable for inspecting completed operations, but the deletion has already happened. It does not meet the requirement to reject an unapproved call before execution.
distractorNotes.b: Deny patterns are genuine enforcement and can block matching commands. A static command pattern does not evaluate a changing approval record, so this choice also blocks the approved use of the same command.
distractorNotes.c: Skills package reusable procedures, but an instruction to invoke a skill is not the automatic execution checkpoint required here. The model could request the maintenance tool without performing that check.

sourceNote: Hook lifecycle; How a hook resolves; PreToolUse decision control

stem: A CI job reviews pull requests from contributor forks with Claude Code. It already runs in an isolated runner with controlled credentials and tool permissions, but standard -p non-interactive runs still discover branch-provided Claude Code hooks and MCP servers. The team wants to skip discovered customizations and supply its trusted review configuration explicitly. Which launch policy best addresses that remaining risk?

options.text: Use standard -p non-interactive mode with pre-approved review tools, retaining configuration discovery so the job can use repository-specific conventions without prompts.
Use bare non-interactive mode (--bare -p), provide API credentials explicitly, and load trusted settings and MCP configuration through their dedicated CLI options.
Use standard -p non-interactive mode with a trusted MCP configuration and --strict-mcp-config, retaining discovered hooks to preserve repository-specific review preparation.
Use standard -p non-interactive mode from an untrusted checkout, relying on interactive workspace and MCP approval records to stop branch-provided startup configuration.

explanation: Bare mode skips automatic discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, CLAUDE.md, and other customizations. Trusted settings and MCP servers can instead be supplied explicitly. For the Anthropic API, bare mode uses an API key or an explicitly configured key helper rather than subscription OAuth credentials. Standard -p runs can execute project Claude Code hooks and connect project MCP servers without workspace or per-server approval prompts. Bare mode reduces this configuration-loading risk; it is not an OS sandbox or a guarantee about code subsequently executed by tools.

distractorNotes.a: Pre-approving tools addresses unattended tool use, not startup discovery. The headless documentation explicitly states that -p otherwise loads the working directory's and user's configured context.
distractorNotes.c: Strict MCP configuration limits which MCP configuration is used, but it does not disable Claude Code hook discovery. The requirement covers both surfaces.
distractorNotes.d: Non-interactive -p runs do not show workspace trust or per-server approval prompts. Interactive trust assumptions therefore do not protect this job from branch-provided hooks and MCP configuration.

sourceNote: Basic usage; Start faster with bare mode

stem: A platform team centrally manages Claude Code on developer workstations. It needs to disable bypass-permissions mode and apply organization-owned Read deny rules for designated secret paths, ignoring permission rules supplied by users, projects, local settings, or --allowedTools. OS-level protection against arbitrary subprocess file access is handled separately. Which deployment meets the Claude Code policy requirement?

options.text: Deploy managed-settings.json in the system directory with the Read deny rules, permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to disable, and allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly enabled.
Distribute the same Read deny rules and bypass-mode setting in developer ~/.claude/settings.json, using fleet configuration management to restore that file after each login.
Commit the Read deny rules and bypass-mode setting in each project's .claude/settings.json, using required code-owner approval to protect policy changes in the central repository.
Publish a trusted settings file and require launcher scripts to pass it with --settings, using the launcher to select permission rules instead of deploying system-managed policy.

explanation: Managed settings apply above user, project, local, and --settings values. The documented deployment example combines Read deny entries, permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: disable, and allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly: true. Together these disable bypass mode and exclude permission rules from lower-trust sources, including --allowedTools. This does not require a prompt for every action or promise universal file confidentiality: the permissions documentation distinguishes built-in file checks and recognized shell operations from arbitrary subprocesses that open files indirectly.

distractorNotes.b: Restoring a user file periodically does not make it managed policy. It remains a user-scope setting rather than the enforced organization-owned source required here.
distractorNotes.c: Repository review protects changes to the central copy, not a developer's local configuration. Project settings do not provide the managed scope or managed-only permission-rule control.
distractorNotes.d: A --settings file is an explicit configuration source, not the managed tier. A launcher convention does not make every developer session consume it or prevent lower-trust permission configuration as required.

sourceNote: Deploy a managed settings file; managed settings precedence

stem: A team placed a detailed repository audit checklist in root CLAUDE.md, bloating ordinary coding sessions. Audits are self-contained: they need repository searches rather than the developer's conversation history, should have read/search tools but no editing tools, and should return findings without adding their intermediate exploration to the main conversation. Which restructuring best meets those constraints?

options.text: Move the checklist into an on-demand skill that runs in the main conversation, leaving the coding session's tools available so the audit can inspect and repair findings together.
Move the checklist into path-scoped project rules for the audited directories, loading it as matching files are inspected and performing the searches in the coding conversation.
Move the checklist into a custom audit subagent with read/search tools and a focused system prompt, delegating each audit with a request for a concise findings report.
Fork the coding conversation for each audit so the worker inherits its current tools and full history, and ask the worker to avoid edits while returning a concise findings report.

explanation: A custom subagent combines a dedicated system prompt, its own context, and an explicitly scoped tool set. The documentation recommends subagents for self-contained work with verbose output and specific tool restrictions. Here, the audit's checklist and intermediate searches belong in that separate context, with findings returned to the main conversation. Ordinary skills provide on-demand instructions but need not isolate execution; a skill configured to run through an appropriately restricted subagent could also meet the requirements, unlike the main-conversation skill offered here.

distractorNotes.a: An ordinary skill reduces always-loaded instructions but runs its exploration in the main conversation. This option also retains editing tools rather than enforcing the required read/search-only tool set.
distractorNotes.b: Path-scoped rules reduce irrelevant instruction loading, but do not create a separate worker context or restrict that worker's tools. The audit's intermediate searches still occupy the coding conversation.
distractorNotes.d: A conversation fork keeps its output separate but inherits the main conversation's tools and history. A request not to edit is not the scoped read/search tool set the scenario requires.

sourceNote: Choose between subagents and main conversation; Write subagent files; Fork the current conversation

stem: During a refactor, Claude Code stops with an auto-compaction thrashing error. A trace shows that compaction succeeds, then another full read of a generated bundle immediately fills the context again. The engineer needs to preserve the current plan and diff while continuing to inspect relevant bundle code. Which recovery addresses both the immediate context pressure and its recurring cause?

options.text: Run /clear and repeat the original refactoring request, then have Claude inspect the complete bundle in the new conversation before reconstructing the implementation plan.
Run /compact with a focus on the plan and diff while dropping the large output, then inspect targeted bundle ranges or delegate the large-file work to a subagent.
Run /compact with a focus on the plan and diff before each retry, retaining whole-bundle reads so each subsequent tool call has the complete source available.
Add the generated directory to .gitignore to reduce repository search noise, then repeat the explicit whole-bundle read in the current conversation to continue the investigation.

explanation: The troubleshooting guide describes this loop as successful compaction followed by immediate refilling from a file or tool output. It recommends reading smaller ranges, compacting with a focus that drops the large output, or moving large-file work to a subagent. Combining focused compaction with a changed inspection strategy retains useful task state and avoids immediately recreating the problem. /clear is a documented fallback when the earlier conversation is no longer needed, which is not this scenario.

distractorNotes.a: Clearing is appropriate when the prior conversation is dispensable. Here it discards needed conversational state, and the repeated whole-bundle read recreates the input pattern that caused thrashing.
distractorNotes.c: Focused compaction addresses the accumulated output, but repeating the same oversized read immediately refills the window. Recovery also needs a narrower read or separate exploration context.
distractorNotes.d: The guide recommends ignoring large build directories for broader performance and search issues. That does not reduce the explicit whole-file read identified here or compact the output already in context.

sourceNote: Performance and stability; Auto-compaction stops with a thrashing error

stem: An engineer is editing an API feature with uncommitted and staged changes. Claude Code should concurrently modify an unrelated migration and its tests. Both workstreams must keep running, but their file edits and staging operations must be separated. The migration does not need the API conversation history. Which setup provides the needed isolation?

options.text: Delegate migration work to a custom subagent using its default working directory, giving it a separate context and instructions to avoid the API feature's files.
Fork the conversation into a second session launched in the same checkout, giving the migration its own message history while retaining the existing local files.
Pause API work, stash the current changes, and let Claude complete the migration in the checkout before restoring the feature work and continuing development.
Start the migration session in its own git worktree using --worktree, with a separate working directory and branch that share the repository's history and remote.

explanation: Worktrees provide separate files and branches while sharing repository history and remote configuration, allowing the two workstreams to proceed without sharing a checkout's edits and staging state. Subagent context isolation or a forked conversation does not by itself supply this filesystem separation. Subagents can also be configured with isolation: worktree, but the default-directory subagent offered here is not configured that way. A new worktree may need its own development-environment setup.

distractorNotes.a: A default subagent starts in the main conversation's current directory. Separate context and cooperative file ownership do not separate the checkout or staging state.
distractorNotes.b: Forking separates conversation state, not the files in the launch directory. Running both sessions in that checkout retains the collision the scenario needs to avoid.
distractorNotes.c: Serializing work through a stash can avoid simultaneous edits, but it pauses the API workstream and therefore fails the concurrency requirement.

sourceNote: Start Claude in a worktree; Resume a worktree session; Isolate subagents with worktrees

stem: Claude Code stops reaching the interactive prompt after a developer changes a personal plugin and project hook. The support engineer wants a reversible comparison that disables customizations while retaining normal authentication, built-in tools, and permissions. Configuration files should remain intact for subsequent diagnosis, and organization-managed hooks and settings must remain in force. Which first step best isolates the suspected customization problem?

options.text: Launch with --safe-mode and compare startup behavior; if it succeeds, use targeted configuration checks to isolate the responsible customization before changing the saved setup.
Launch with --debug and reproduce the startup failure under the existing configuration, collecting event logs before comparing the hook and plugin definitions on disk.
Run claude doctor from the shell and correct reported installation or settings errors, then retry startup with the existing customizations still enabled for the session.
Point CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR at a fresh directory and launch outside the project, redoing first-run setup and authentication before comparing behavior with the usual configuration.

explanation: Safe mode provides the requested comparison: it disables customizations while normal authentication, model selection, built-in tools, and permissions continue to work. Organization-managed hooks and settings policy still apply. If startup succeeds, targeted checks can narrow the customization responsible. This is different from a fresh configuration directory, which also changes user setup and requires authentication, and from diagnostics that observe the existing configuration without disabling it.

distractorNotes.b: Debug logging is useful evidence and may help later, but it does not supply the requested comparison with customizations disabled.
distractorNotes.c: The shell doctor command provides read-only installation and settings diagnostics without starting a session. It does not create a customization-disabled comparison, and fixing files first changes the saved setup.
distractorNotes.d: A clean configuration directory is a useful broader isolation test, but it changes user settings and triggers first-run authentication. Safe mode more closely preserves the baseline required here.

sourceNote: Check resolved settings; Check hooks; Test against a clean configuration

stem: A team wants a version-controlled release-preparation runbook that developers invoke as a slash command. Its detailed steps should load on demand, and because timing matters, Claude must not invoke the runbook automatically when a discussion merely mentions a release. Which configuration best meets the invocation and context requirements?

options.text: Create a project skill with default invocation settings and a precise description saying to use it when release preparation is requested, keeping the body out of startup context.
Create a project skill with user-invocable set to false and a release-specific description, leaving its procedure available for Claude to discover when the conversation is relevant.
Create .claude/skills/release-prep/SKILL.md with disable-model-invocation: true, retaining developer slash-command invocation while loading its body when the developer invokes it.
Create a project skill with context: fork so release preparation runs in a separate subagent, leaving its default invocation settings to support discovery and direct slash commands.

explanation: A project skill packages the version-controlled runbook and exposes its slash command. By default both Claude and the user can invoke skills. Setting disable-model-invocation: true disables Claude's automatic invocation while preserving explicit developer invocation; its description is not placed in context, and the full body loads when the user invokes it. This controls invocation of the skill, not authorization of every underlying release operation, which still needs appropriate tool and system permissions.

distractorNotes.a: Default skills load their bodies on demand, but Claude can invoke them automatically. A careful description guides selection rather than disabling model invocation.
distractorNotes.b: user-invocable: false does the opposite of the requirement: it removes the user's slash-command invocation while leaving the skill available to Claude.
distractorNotes.d: context: fork selects execution in a subagent. It does not disable automatic invocation, so execution isolation is not a substitute for controlling who starts the runbook.

sourceNote: Choose where skills load; Control who invokes a skill; Run skills in a subagent

stem: An internal MCP server queries database schemas over stdio. After verbose diagnostics are enabled, the client reports malformed messages and some requests time out. A captured stream shows plain-text connection logs interleaved with otherwise valid newline-delimited JSON-RPC responses. The team must retain diagnostics and compatibility with unmodified MCP clients. Which remediation targets the demonstrated protocol defect?

options.text: Flush stdout after each connection log and JSON-RPC response so the client receives complete lines promptly, preserving the existing shared stream for diagnostics and results.
Serialize each diagnostic as a standalone JSON string on stdout before continuing JSON-RPC responses, ensuring the client encounters syntactically valid JSON on each line.
Serialize writes under a shared output lock so connection logs and JSON-RPC responses cannot interleave within a line, retaining both kinds of output on the same stream.
Send diagnostic logs to stderr and reserve stdout for valid newline-delimited MCP messages, including output produced by imported libraries and server startup routines.

explanation: The stdio binding reserves stdout for valid MCP messages, one JSON-RPC message per line, and explicitly permits informational, debug, and error logging on stderr. The observed connection logs violate that contract even if they are flushed promptly or written without byte-level interleaving. Routing them to stderr preserves diagnostics without changing the client protocol. The specification establishes the violation, not a guaranteed timeout duration or a universal client response to malformed input.

distractorNotes.a: Flushing can address delayed delivery, but prompt delivery does not make plain-text log lines valid MCP messages. The demonstrated defect remains.
distractorNotes.b: Valid JSON syntax is insufficient: a standalone JSON string is not a JSON-RPC request, response, or notification. Diagnostic encoding must not violate the MCP message contract.
distractorNotes.c: A lock can prevent bytes from concurrent writers corrupting one another, but complete plain-text log lines still violate the stdout message contract.

sourceNote: stdio message framing and standard-stream rules; Receiving Messages
